title: Immigration advocates: There’s more work to do to protect Marylanders
summary: A ban on immigration enforcement agreements signed into law this week ended years of struggle for immigrant advocates, but they were back in Annapolis Friday to say the struggle is not over when it comes or protecting immigrant communities.
content:
by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters February 20, 2026

by William J. Ford, Maryland Matters February 20, 2026

A ban on immigration enforcement agreements in Maryland that was signed into law this week ended years of struggle for immigrant advocates, but they were back in Annapolis Friday to say the struggle is not over when it comes to protecting immigrant communities.

Specifically, they said, it is time to end all collaboration with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the agency known as ICE.

“We will demand that Maryland stops our role in ICE devastating our communities,” said Ama Frimpong, legal director for We Are CASA. “We will demand that Maryland plays no role in tearing apart families, kidnapping our hard-working parents, shattering the dreams of our innocent children causing fear and terror in our communities. Cut all ties with ICE in the state of Maryland.”

A CASA rally scheduled for Lawyers Mall was forced inside by Friday’s rain, to a room inside the House of Delegates office building across the street.

After years of advocates arguing that local police should not be doing the work of federal agents, a bill signing was held Tuesday to prohibit so-called 287(g) agreements between ICE and local law enforcement agencies.

Moore signs bills banning agreements between local police, federal immigration agencies

But advocates such as Dana Vickers Shelly, executive director with the ACLU of Maryland, said one measure alone would not increase trust between public agencies and immigrant communities, or ensure due process.

“We need policies that uplift the humanity of every Marylander, policies that build trust between neighbors and local institutions … regardless of the color of our skin, regardless of where we were born [and] where we live now,” she said.

Vickers Shelly specifically highlighted Senate Bill 791 and House Bill 1575 – also known as “The Community Trust Act” – sponsored by Sen. Clarence Lam (D-Anne Arundel and Howard) and Del. N. Scott Phillips (D-Baltimore County). Phillips chairs the Legislative Black Caucus, which made the Trust Act and 287(g) bills two of its many priorities for this year’s session.

The pending bills seek to close a loophole that would ban local law enforcement agencies and jails to detain any individuals based on immigration status and responding to requests from ICE.

The one exception would be from a “judicial warrant.” That would not include administrative warrants from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Justice, “or any successor agency.”

Current law allows local law enforcement agencies to assist ICE through jail transfers and can detain individuals without a warrant from a judge.

“In America, we live by a set of rules. Unfortunately, what we see today, people aren’t abiding by any of those rules,” Phillips said at the CASA rally. “In the Constitution, when it talks about due process, it doesn’t say for some. It says for all.”

Hearings on both bills are scheduled Wednesday before the Senate Judicial Proceedings and House Judiciary committees.

Another measure advocates are pushing for is the “Data Privacy Act,” which proposes to close loopholes in the state’s current Public Information Act. Senate Bill 504 and House Bill 711, sponsored respectively by Lam and Del. Lorig Charkoudian (D-Montgomery), would prohibit a business from selling personal data of an individual “for the purpose of immigration enforcement.”

The data bills highlight three agencies – the Motor Vehicle Administration, the Maryland State Police and the Department of Public Safety and Correctional Services – and directs them to “adopt regulations and procedures to implement, enforce and ensure compliance.”

The bills say an agency, company, or a person processing personal data would still need to comply with any civil, criminal or regulatory investigation issued by a subpoena or summons.

Charkoudian said at Friday’s rally that some corporations are willing to “sell out to fascism and authoritarianism” under the current federal government.

“We are going to say this session, ‘No, you will not,’” she said.

The House version is scheduled for a hearing Tuesday before Economic Matters Committee and the Senate bill Thursday before the Finance Committee.

But Republican legislators say federal immigration authorities are permitted under constitutional and federal law to operate in the U.S. House Minority Leader Jason Buckel (R-Allegany) said agencies such as ICE and the FBI are able to track down individuals with violent and extensive criminal records that way.

Buckel said no one supports the tragedies that happened last month in Minnesota, where two Americans were fatally shot by federal immigration agents who had been deployed to the city.

“But that doesn’t mean that you can say we’re not going to have lawful enforcement of our nation’s immigration laws in Maryland because we don’t like ICE. That’s absurd,” he said.
